lines.text: Europe's last pagan state became one of its largest, vanished from the map, and sang its way back to freedom. This is the story of Lithuania.
In 1203 Mindaugas was born, the warrior prince who would become the first and only crowned king of Lithuania.
By the 1230s the Lithuanian lands were drawing together into a grand duchy, a state that would grow enormous.
In 1253 Mindaugas was crowned king, and Lithuania entered the written history of Europe.
Gediminas, born in 1275, would be the grand duke who made Vilnius his capital.
In 1323 Vilnius was named for the first time in his letters, the city whose baroque old town still stands.
Under Grand Duke Vytautas, born in 1350, Lithuania would stretch from the Baltic almost to the Black Sea.
In 1410, at Grunwald, Lithuania and Poland together crushed the Teutonic Knights, one of the great battles of medieval Europe.
In 1569 the two joined as one Commonwealth, with an elected king, and for a time it was among Europe's largest states.
Ten years later Vilnius University was founded, one of the oldest in this part of Europe.
But from 1772 Russia, Prussia and Austria carved up the Commonwealth, and by 1795 it was gone, and Lithuania fell under Russian rule.
On the sixteenth of February 1918, as the First World War raged, Lithuania declared its independence.
It lasted barely twenty years. In 1940 the Soviet Union occupied the Baltic states, and returned again in 1944.
In 1964 Gitanas Nauseda was born, who would be president of a free Lithuania from 2019.
That same year came Arvydas Sabonis, one of the greatest basketball players Europe has ever produced.
From 1987 huge crowds across the Baltic sang their national songs, a peaceful revolution against Soviet rule.
In August 1989 some two million people joined hands in a human chain across three countries, the Baltic Way.
On the eleventh of March 1990, Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare itself free.
In January 1991 Soviet troops attacked the television tower in Vilnius, but the people held firm.
And in 2004 Lithuania joined the European Union with nine other countries, its place in Europe secure.
From pagan kings to a free member of Europe, Lithuania kept its song alive.
